To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll stay at 20k for game 72, read the last two reviews, and focus on securing broad bases with two separate eyes before starting new groups. I’ll save the moves and a review for the next session.

# Game 71: Black vs 20k — W+R

Played 2026-10-06. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Resigned after White54 J7; board() confirmed W+R. No numerical score or official dead-stone adjudication.
Physical captures: Black1, White2. White44 A2 captured A3/A4; Black49 A1 captured B1.
Final displayed stones: Black25, White26. Black had upper9, lower15 and isolatedA1.
20k record: fourteen wins, fifty losses, three draws. Retain20k; repeatable strength is not established.

## Records and verification

Read70/69 and consulted35 before choosing20k.
game-071-log.json contains selection, all27 play responses, resignation, final confirmation, complete returned boards, current-position inventories, provisional manual notes, exact moves and actual-history verification.
game-071.sgf records all54 moves and W+R.

All54 moves matched30 full board/capture/returned-ko checks.
Black27 placements−2 captured=25; White27 placements−1 captured=26.
No pass, refused move or attempted recapture. Black49 created transient B1 ko; White50 C8 cleared it before the returned board.
Code did not select, rank or recommend moves or search hypothetical sequences. Choices and hypothetical reading were manual.
Provisional notes in the log are not proof of life, secured area or optimal play; this review qualifies them.

Exact moves:
1 B C3, 2 W E5, 3 B G7, 4 W C4, 5 B D3, 6 W D4, 7 B G3, 8 W G4, 9 B C7, 10 W E3, 11 B E7, 12 W E6, 13 B C2, 14 W E2, 15 B G2, 16 W D2, 17 B F7, 18 W B3, 19 B B2, 20 W B4, 21 B A3, 22 W C6, 23 B A4, 24 W A5, 25 B G6, 26 W B7, 27 B D7, 28 W G5, 29 B H3, 30 W H4, 31 B D6, 32 W C5, 33 B F6, 34 W F5, 35 B F2, 36 W H1, 37 B F1, 38 W F3, 39 B H2, 40 W H6, 41 B J3, 42 W J1, 43 B E1, 44 W A2, 45 B D1, 46 W B1, 47 B C1, 48 W A3, 49 B A1, 50 W C8, 51 B H7, 52 W J6, 53 B J4, 54 W J7.

## Four broad footholds needed too many boundary turns

C3 met White E5. G7 took the opposite corner.
D3 directly joined C3 under C4, then White D4 pressed the chain.
G3 at7 and C7 at9 established the other two corners.
The conditional whole bottom27 plus top27 outline was54, but most boundaries, bridges and eyes were unplayed.

White E3 at10 immediately split the bottom.
E7 at11 broadened the top; White E6 pressed it.
C2/G2 retained lower second-line points while joined.
White E2/D2 then occupied the central bottom route.
F7 at17 actually joined E7/G7, while C7 remained separate until D7 at27.

At18 the explicit provisional outline was upper27 + lower-left10 (A/B/C rows1–3 nine plus D3) + lower-right9 (G/H/J rows1–3) =46.
This already had only one coordinate of margin above Black45, and none of the three regions had completed two-eye proof.
White B3, already on the board at18, directly contested a point inside the lower-left outline.
Excluding already-White B3 leaves at most45, with zero reduction margin and life still unproved.
The log called this conditional; it was still too optimistic to use as a viable territorial plan.
Earlier51 also included unplayed lower-left D1/D2; White D2 at16 invalidated that count.
Replace such shorthand immediately rather than carrying its apparent margin forward.

The strategic problem was spending turns on separated footholds without a complete boundary schedule for any threatened lower base.
Four corners and connected third-line stones did not imply four living regions.
No optimal opening, winning substitution or individual move value is established.

## A3/A4 extended a base without a verified second eye

White B3 at18 left C3/D3/C2 only B2/C1.
B2 at19 extended the joined group; White B4 correctly connected B3 to C4/D4.
That lower group now had A2/B1/C1.
A3 at21 was separate with A2/A4. The immediate A4 cap was considered but no forced saving schedule was found.
White instead C6 at22 allowed A4 at23 to join A3.
White A5 at24 left BOTH A3/A4 soleA2.

A4 preserved two actual edge stones but did not provide a second eye or connect them to the lower main.
This was the point to reassess the plan before extending: A5 was an immediate, known cap.
The game stopped additions there after24; it did not turn the earlier extensions into a successful sacrifice.
White A2 at44 captured both and reopened A3/A4 for adjacent White groups.
Those two physical captures are distinct from later life judgments.

Direct A2 would have joined the six stones then present but consumed the bridge/space; the remaining A1/B1/C1 region was connected and its D1 boundary was unplayed.
No verified earlier two-eye repair is claimed.
Do not repeat a known cap merely because the new stone currently has a liberty.

## Real gains and connections did not secure enough living room

G6 at25 joined G7 and expanded below the original top outline.
D7 at27 joined C7 to E7/main.
D6 at31 and F6 at33 added joined boundary points; F6 also connected F7/G6.

The immediate White D1 block was considered; it would have denied that route.
Actual White A2 captured A3/A4 instead, allowing D1 at45.
White B1 then left the four lower-left stones soleC1.
C1 at47 promptly saved and joined them to the right group through D1/E1/F1.
This was an actual rescue of connection; it did not prove life.
White A3 at48 connected A2 to B3/full left enemy, denying the hoped-for isolated A2 capture.

## A1 was a ko capture, not a second unconditional eye

After C1, isolated White B1 had only A1.
Black A1 at49 captured it, but Black A1 itself had ONLY B1.
The actual replay infers simple ko at B1 immediately after49.

B2/C2/C3/D3/C1/D1/E1/F1/F2/G2/G3/H2/H3/J3/J4.

B1 was surrounded by Black but was NOT an unconditional eye: White B1 captures isolated A1.
That hypothetical one-stone capture would leave White B1 soleA1 and create simple ko at A1.
Do not treat the raw flood-fill ownership of B1 as life.

Limited final lower reading:
Black J2 would contain White H1/J1 to soleG1. White G1 would be suicide because the complete Black lower group still has B1/J5. Black G1 can then capture both.
Conversely Black G1 contains them to soleJ2; White J2 would be suicide for the same reason, and Black J2 captures both.
In either order the opened H1/J1 points are ONE adjacent two-point region.
Filling H1 would leave only J1, not create two eyes.
This is a local capture/eye-space check, not an exhaustive death proof: J5 access and ko threats still exist.
No unconditional lower life was established before resignation.

## Upper invasion and resignation limits

White B7 at26 contested the left upper boundary.
White C8 at50 entered with B8/D8/C9; it was separate from B7.
H7 at51 joined G7 and contained White H6.
White J6 at52 joined H6; J4 at53 added a connected lower boundary point.
White J7 at54 joined H6/J6 and reduced the upper right.

Final upper Black9: C7/D7/D6/E7/F7/F6/G6/G7/H7.
Liberties D8/D5/E8/F8/G8/H8.
No completed two-eye divider was present.
White upper-right H6/J6/J7 had H5/J5/J8 and could still reach its central group through H5.
The upper group may develop life in the open top region; it is not declared dead.
The lower group likewise is not called exhaustively dead.
Resignation judged the position strategically unrecoverable with inadequate proved living area and continuing invasion pressure.
There is no numerical final score, official area total or scored dead-stone list.

Raw current-board flood-fill was Black26/White29/neutral26.
It retains every displayed stone and falsely treats B1 as unconditional Black territory.
It is an inventory, not an independent final score; do not attach a numerical loss margin to it.
Game52's separate scoring discrepancy remains unresolved.

## Carry forward

Retain20k: fourteen wins, fifty losses, three draws.
Read71/70 next; consult69 for capped bases and35/30 for broad development.
Count the room that a complete eye/connection schedule can actually retain, not a sum of four corner rectangles.
At18 even the optimistic46 had almost no margin and contained White B3.
A3/A4 met the anticipated A5 cap without creating life; identify the second room before spending that extension turn.
E1/D1/C1 was a real rescue route allowed by actual replies, but physical connection still lacked unconditional eyes.
A1 capture was a temporary ko; isolated A1 made B1 a false eye.
H1/J1 capture opens one adjacent room, not two; filling its divider cannot manufacture a second room.
Inspect complete enemy groups: A3 joined A2 to the left main, and C5/F5 correctly joined the larger enemies.
No saving move or winning alternate opening was verified. Improve the schedule before increasing opponent strength.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
